evals.prompt: I need to add a short-sequence fast path to TensorRT-LLM's MLA attention: for DSA models, which today run context attention through the sparse absorbed (MQA) path, short contexts should use dense MHA instead. A synthetic, trimmed excerpt of the repo is at /workspace/input/trtllm-mini (it is not runnable). There is no GPU, no full TensorRT-LLM checkout, and no network in this environment; do not clone, download, or install anything. Before any code is written, work out which existing code this should reuse and what could go wrong, then give me a short implementation plan. Do not write the implementation.
evals.expected_output: Explores the whole MLA class (all methods, forward_* paths, __init__ invariants) before designing, then recommends creating self.mha for DSA models and dispatching short contexts to the existing dense context path through the forward_context() dispatcher rather than forward_context_default(), which ignores cached KV. Updates the `assert self.mha is None` invariant instead of adding a parallel attribute, and keeps the plan inside tensorrt_llm/_torch/.
assertions: Inspects the whole MLA class in tensorrt_llm/_torch/attention/mla.py before designing: enumerates its methods (e.g., grep -n "def ") and reads the existing forward_* implementations, not only the method it plans to change.

Recommends reusing the existing dense context-attention path (the TrtllmAttention-backed MHA used by forward_context / forward_context_default) instead of writing a new attention computation such as an SDPA loop or a new forward_context_short_mha method.

Recommends dispatching through forward_context() rather than calling forward_context_default() directly, because forward_context_default() does not handle contexts with cached KV tokens (cached-KV / chunked-prefill paths).

Proposes creating self.mha for DSA models (reusing the existing attribute instead of adding a parallel one such as self._short_seq_mha) and changing the `assert self.mha is None` invariant (e.g., to assert self.mqa is not None) rather than working around it.
Keeps all proposed changes inside tensorrt_llm/_torch/ and does not propose modifying the engine-building layer in tensorrt_llm/layers/attention.py.

evals.prompt: I'm adding a new context-attention path for MLA in TensorRT-LLM's PyTorch backend and planned to write two helpers for it: (1) a @torch.compile-wrapped fast_cat(a, b) to concatenate k_nope with the per-head expanded k_pe, and (2) apply_rope(q, k_pe, position_ids), because I don't see RoPE applied anywhere in forward_context_default. A synthetic, trimmed excerpt of the repo is at /workspace/input/trtllm-mini (not runnable; there is no GPU, no full checkout, and no network, so do not clone or install anything). Should I write either helper? Tell me what to use instead and why.
evals.expected_output: Finds maybe_compiled_cat (built on maybe_compile) in tensorrt_llm/_torch/utils.py, already used for this exact concatenation, and recommends it over a new compiled helper. Traces RoPE handling to apply_rotary_emb = not rope_fusion and to the fused TrtllmAttention kernel (apply_rope=self.rope_fusion with latent_cache), concluding that Python RoPE in the new path would double-apply it, so neither helper should be written.
assertions: Finds maybe_compiled_cat (decorated with maybe_compile) in tensorrt_llm/_torch/utils.py, already used for the same k_nope/k_pe concatenation in forward_context_default, and recommends reusing it instead of a new torch.compile helper.
Traces where RoPE is handled: _project_qkv applies self.rotary_emb only when apply_rotary_emb is True, and apply_rotary_emb is set to `not rope_fusion`.

Concludes that with rope_fusion enabled the fused attention kernel applies RoPE itself (TrtllmAttention passes apply_rope=self.rope_fusion together with latent_cache), so adding apply_rope in the new path would apply RoPE twice.
Recommends writing neither helper: reuse maybe_compiled_cat and the existing RoPE handling (the existing RotaryEmbedding only matters when rope_fusion is disabled).

evals.prompt: My new unit test for TensorRT-LLM's MLA module (PyTorch backend) builds an MLA module, fills module.kv_b_proj.weight with a random tensor in the HuggingFace checkpoint shape [num_heads * (qk_nope_head_dim + v_head_dim), kv_lora_rank], and compares the output against a reference implementation that uses the same HF-shaped weight. The outputs don't match, especially once generation tokens are in the batch. I also assemble AttentionMetadata by hand. A synthetic, trimmed excerpt of the repo is at /workspace/input/trtllm-mini (not runnable; there is no GPU or network, so don't clone or install anything). What is likely wrong, and how should the test set things up instead?
evals.expected_output: Explains that TensorRT-LLM transforms kv_b_proj at load time (load_kv_b_proj_and_k_b_proj_trans shards by head and derives k_b_proj_trans and v_b_proj, which the absorption/generation path reads), so overwriting kv_b_proj.weight with an HF-layout tensor leaves the module inconsistent. The test should initialize weights in the loaded layout, e.g., through the production loader or load_mla_weights_for_test, and build metadata with the existing helpers in attention_test_utils.py.
assertions: Identifies that TensorRT-LLM transforms the HF kv_b_proj weight at load time, pointing to load_kv_b_proj_and_k_b_proj_trans in tensorrt_llm/_torch/models/modeling_deepseekv3.py (head sharding plus the derived k_b_proj_trans and v_b_proj tensors).

Explains that the generation/absorption path (forward_absorption) reads k_b_proj_trans and v_b_proj, which remain uninitialized when only kv_b_proj.weight is overwritten, consistent with the mismatch appearing once generation tokens are present.

Recommends initializing test weights in TensorRT-LLM's loaded layout (e.g., passing HF-format weights through the production loader or load_mla_weights_for_test) rather than copying HF-layout tensors directly into module parameters.
Recommends replacing the hand-built AttentionMetadata with the existing helpers in tests/unittest/_torch/attention/attention_test_utils.py (e.g., create_test_metadata).

evals.prompt: I'm about to implement a new 'attention sinks + sliding window' option in TensorRT-LLM's attention module. I don't have the repository available right now (there is no checkout and no network in this environment, so don't try to clone anything). Before I write any code, give me the concrete exploration checklist I should run first: specific grep commands and files, and what I'm looking for at each step.
evals.expected_output: A step-by-step exploration checklist scoped to the PyTorch backend (tensorrt_llm/_torch/): map the whole class (all methods, __init__ attributes, hierarchy), read every forward method, search existing backends and utilities by concept, check what the fused kernels in attention/backends already handle, review assertions, check weight layouts, and trace callers/dispatchers and get_sm_version() gates, each with concrete grep commands.
assertions: Scopes the exploration to the PyTorch backend under tensorrt_llm/_torch/ and explicitly sets the TensorRT backend aside.

Starts by mapping the whole class (listing all methods, e.g., grep -n "def ", plus __init__ attributes and the class hierarchy such as Attention / MLA / TrtllmAttention) and reading every existing forward method in full, not just signatures.

Includes searching for existing implementations by concept rather than only exact names (e.g., grep -rn over tensorrt_llm/_torch/ for window/sink/mask keywords) and checking what the fused attention backends in tensorrt_llm/_torch/attention/backends/ already handle, including C++ kernels behind the bindings, before writing Python.
Includes grepping the existing assert statements/invariants in the class and treating them as things to update if the new path invalidates them, rather than working around them.
Includes tracing the callers of any method it plans to reuse to find the higher-level dispatcher, and checking get_sm_version() hardware gates near those call sites.
